title: Bias and Representational Harm in LLMs

questions.question: How does the lesson distinguish representational harm from allocational harm?
options: Representational harm only matters for vision models
Representational harm is stereotypes / erasure / demeaning portrayal; allocational harm is unequal material outcomes for a group
Representational is computational; allocational is statistical
Allocational harm only occurs offline
questions.explanation: The lesson defines representational harm as stereotypes, erasure, or demeaning portrayal (e.g. depicting nurses as exclusively female), while allocational harm is unequal material outcomes for a group (e.g. scoring one group's resumes systematically lower) -- a model can be biased on one axis without the other.

questions.question: Which of these are the three evaluation-metric categories from Gallegos et al. 2024?
options: Pre-RLHF, mid-RLHF, post-RLHF
Vision, audio, text
WEAT, BLEU, ROUGE
Embedding-based, probability-based, generated-text-based
questions.explanation: Gallegos et al. 2024, as the lesson describes it, categorize bias-evaluation metrics into embedding-based (WEAT-style association tests), probability-based (stereotype-confirming vs violating completion likelihoods), and generated-text-based (downstream-task measurement on generated output).

questions.question: Why is intersectional fairness evaluation needed in addition to single-axis evaluation?
options: Intersectionality is the same as cross-validation
Single-axis measures are computationally cheaper
Single-axis is the only legally allowed approach
Bias that only emerges at intersections (e.g., gender x race) is missed by evaluations that look at one axis at a time
questions.explanation: The lesson's An et al. 2025 example shows Black women scoring best and Black men scoring worst on automated resume evaluation -- a pattern invisible to gender-only or race-only evaluation and detectable only by looking at the gender x race intersection.

questions.question: What does WinoIdentity (COLM 2025) introduce?
options: An adversarial attack on demographic classifiers
A new tokenizer for identity terms
A replacement for WEAT in embedding space

Uncertainty-based intersectional fairness evaluation for coreference resolution, comparing the model's uncertainty over pronoun-referent choices across intersectional identity tuples, not just point predictions
questions.explanation: The lesson describes WinoIdentity as extending Winogender/WinoBias-style coreference-resolution bias evaluation to intersectional identities with an uncertainty-based fairness measure, testing whether the model's confidence over pronoun-referent choices differs across intersectional identity tuples, not just whether it gets the point prediction right.

questions.question: Which of these is a mechanistic-interpretability approach to bias?
options: Switching to DPO from PPO
Identifying gender-correlated FFN-value/FFN-query/attention-value neurons, or using SAEs to surface race-correlated features
Adding more KL regularization
Re-labeling the training set
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Yu & Ananiadou 2025 identifying gender-correlated neurons in FFN-value, FFN-query, and attention-value layers, and Ahsan & Wallace 2025 using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to surface race-correlated features -- both mechanistic interventions on the model's internals rather than training-process changes.

questions.question: What does the 10-year meta-critique (arXiv:2508.11067) argue about the bias literature?
options: It disproportionately focuses on binary-gender bias, neglecting other axes (disability, religion, migration status, multi-lingual identity) that may harm marginalized groups by neglect
It avoids quantitative methods
It overemphasizes intersectionality
It is balanced across all identity axes
questions.explanation: The lesson summarizes the meta-critique as finding that a decade of bias literature disproportionately focuses on binary-gender bias, while axes like disability, religion, migration status, and multi-lingual identity receive far less attention -- risking harm to those groups through neglect.
